reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma
clinicalPearls: Presents as a painful arc during mid-range abduction, typically with anterolateral shoulder pain that is worse on overhead reach and at night when lying on the affected side.
The term subacromial pain syndrome is increasingly preferred, reflecting a shift away from a purely mechanical model towards a spectrum including bursitis, tendinopathy and partial cuff pathology.
Neer and Hawkins-Kennedy provocation tests are sensitive but not specific; a positive subacromial injection test supports the diagnosis by transiently abolishing pain and improving cuff strength.
Acromial morphology matters: a hooked (Bigliami type III) acromion and a laterally downsloping acromion are associated with increased mechanical narrowing of the subacromial space.

Distinguish primary (extrinsic mechanical) impingement from secondary impingement arising from glenohumeral instability or scapular dyskinesis, as the latter requires rehabilitation rather than decompression.
Structured physiotherapy targeting rotator cuff and scapular stabiliser strengthening is first-line and resolves symptoms in the majority without surgery.
Consider an alternative or coexisting diagnosis when weakness is profound or there is loss of active elevation, suggesting a full-thickness cuff tear rather than isolated impingement.
Subacromial corticosteroid injection can provide short-term relief and aid engagement with rehabilitation, but repeated injections risk tendon deterioration.
reference.pathophysiology: Impingement describes mechanical compression and irritation of the rotator cuff tendons (chiefly supraspinatus) and the subacromial bursa within the coracoacromial arch during elevation of the arm. Extrinsic factors include acromial shape, subacromial spurs and coracoacromial ligament thickening, which narrow the outlet, while intrinsic tendon degeneration, hypovascularity of the critical zone and age-related collagen changes weaken the tendon. Dynamic contributors such as scapular dyskinesis, glenohumeral instability and rotator cuff or periscapular muscle imbalance reduce effective humeral head depression, allowing superior migration and repetitive abrasion. The resulting inflammatory and degenerative cascade produces bursitis, tendinopathy and progressive partial tearing, forming part of a continuum that may culminate in cuff failure.
additionalDifferentials: Rotator cuff tear (partial or full thickness)
Cervical radiculopathy referring to the shoulder
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs including an outlet (scapular Y) view to assess acromial morphology and spurs
Ultrasound of the rotator cuff and subacromial bursa, including dynamic assessment during elevation
MRI to characterise cuff tendinopathy, partial or full-thickness tears and bursal changes
Diagnostic subacromial local anaesthetic injection test
Assessment of scapular kinematics and posture
Cervical spine imaging if radicular features are present
redFlags: Profound weakness or inability to actively elevate the arm suggesting a large or massive cuff tear
Rest and night pain unresponsive to conservative measures raising concern for tumour or infection
History of significant trauma with acute loss of function suggesting acute cuff rupture or fracture
Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss or a palpable mass
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve substantially with a sustained programme of physiotherapy and activity modification, and outcomes of subacromial decompression are comparable to structured exercise in appropriately selected cases. Prognosis is less favourable when impingement is secondary to unaddressed instability, dyskinesis or an established cuff tear.
pitfalls: Attributing all anterolateral shoulder pain to impingement while missing an underlying full-thickness cuff tear or glenohumeral pathology.
Proceeding to acromioplasty without first correcting scapular dyskinesis or instability, leading to persistent secondary impingement.
Over-reliance on radiographic acromial shape, which correlates poorly with symptoms in individual patients.
Repeated corticosteroid injections that mask progression and may compromise tendon integrity.
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma
British Elbow and Shoulder Society guidance on subacromial pain
management: First-line structured physiotherapy targeting rotator cuff and scapular stabiliser strengthening, combined with activity modification
Analgesia and NSAIDs for symptom control
Subacromial corticosteroid injection for refractory pain, used judiciously
Manage secondary impingement from scapular dyskinesis or glenohumeral instability with rehabilitation rather than decompression
Correct posture and scapular kinematics with a graded return to overhead activity
Surgical subacromial decompression, with treatment of any cuff pathology, reserved for those failing sustained conservative therapy
Referral to orthopaedics or physiotherapy where symptoms persist or a rotator cuff tear is suspected
